paragraphs.text: Wolfram syndrome-2 is an autosomal recessive form of Wolfram syndrome. El-Shanti et al. (2000) noted that only insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and optic atrophy are needed to diagnose Wolfram syndrome. In the families they studied, the WFS2 phenotype differed from the classic syndrome in 2 ways: none of the affected members had diabetes insipidus, and several patients had profound upper gastrointestinal ulceration and bleeding. Mozzillo et al. (2014) also described defective platelet aggregation in WFS2.

paragraphs.text: Mozzillo et al. (2014) reported a Caucasian girl with WFS2, the first child of parents who said they were not consanguineous. She had had recurrent bleeding upper intestinal ulcers since age 5 years. At age 14, she was diagnosed with malrotation and partial duodenal intussusception and underwent resection of a duodenal tract with duodenal-jejunal anastomosis. At age 16, she developed reduced visual acuity and dyschromatopsia. Best corrected visual acuity was 20/40 in the right eye and 20/50 in the left. Fundus examination showed optic disc pallor with preserved pupillary light reflexes, pattern visual evoked potentials were normal, and brain MRI showed normal optic nerve caliber. Non-autoimmune diabetes developed at age 17 years, and she started insulin. Further studies found bilateral sensorineural hearing loss in the high frequencies, slow intestinal transit, and entero-gastric bile reflux. Visual findings were unchanged after 5 years of follow-up. Visual field testing, ERG, and OCT of the macula and retinal nerve fiber layer then showed moderate involvement of the optic nerve in both eyes. The authors considered this compatible with optic neuropathy and excluded optic atrophy. Platelet aggregation to ADP was reduced and reversible up to 10 microM, and platelet secretion in response to ADP was absent. Responses to collagen, epinephrine, and ristocetin were normal. At age 22 years, she had diabetes, optic neuropathy with preserved visual acuity, tinnitus from the high-frequency hearing loss, bile reflux, slow intestinal transit, defective platelet aggregation to ADP, and bleeding upper intestinal ulcers. Her parents and brother, who were heterozygous carriers, had no ophthalmologic abnormalities, diabetes, or deafness, but they did have a reversible platelet aggregation defect in response to ADP.

paragraphs.text: Mozzillo et al. (2014) suggested that the 'asymptomatic' optic atrophy reported in Jordanian WFS2 patients may also have been optic neuropathy. Because optic atrophy is a main diagnostic criterion for Wolfram syndrome, they suggested that the so-called WFS2 might not be a subtype of Wolfram syndrome. They also noted that their patient had impaired platelet aggregation to ADP rather than to collagen, as had been reported in the Jordanian patients. Since both collagen- and ADP-induced aggregation are calcium-mediated, they proposed that different experimental conditions or variability between patients could explain the difference.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of 3 consanguineous Jordanian families with WFS2, Amr et al. (2007) identified a homozygous mutation in the ZCD2 gene (CISD2): a G-to-C transversion at nucleotide 109 predicting a glu37-to-gln (E37Q) substitution. The amino acid is conserved, but the authors concluded that the mutation caused disease by aberrant splicing. The mutation removed exon 2 from the mRNA and introduced a premature stop codon. They found no mutations in the gene when they screened 377 probands with hearing loss.

paragraphs.text: In a Caucasian girl with WFS2, Mozzillo et al. (2014) identified a homozygous intragenic deletion in the CISD2 gene that removed exon 2. They found it by PCR and cDNA sequencing and confirmed it by SNP-array analysis. Her parents and brother were heterozygous for the deletion. The parents said they were not consanguineous, and runs of homozygosity showed no parental relationship, but microsatellite analysis supported a common ancestor.

paragraphs.text: In a Caucasian girl with Wolfram syndrome-2, Mozzillo et al. (2014) identified a homozygous intragenic deletion that removed all of CISD2 exon 2. Using SNP-array analysis, they estimated a minimum deletion size of 739 bp and restricted the maximum to a 2,050-bp region spanning from intron 2 to intron 3. The deleted region included the codons for amino acids 102 to 106 within the 2Fe-2S domain, which the authors suggested may produce a nonfunctional protein. Her parents and brother were heterozygous and had no ophthalmologic abnormalities, diabetes, or deafness, but they had a reversible platelet aggregation defect in response to ADP.

checks.claim: Mozzillo et al. (2014) identified a homozygous intragenic deletion removing all of CISD2 exon 2 in a Caucasian girl with Wolfram syndrome-2.
checks.evidence_quote: CISD2 cDNA sequencing revealed a novel homozygous deletion affecting the whole exon 2 of CISD2
checks.explanation: Stated; patient is Caucasian girl with WFS2.

checks.claim: Using SNP-array analysis, Mozzillo et al. (2014) estimated a minimum size of 739 bp for the CISD2 exon 2 deletion.
checks.evidence_quote: The minimum size of deletion was 739 bp while the maximum size was 4,250 bp.

checks.claim: Mozzillo et al. (2014) restricted the maximum extent of the CISD2 exon 2 deletion to a 2,050-bp region spanning intron 2 to intron 3.
checks.evidence_quote: Thus, the maximum deletion size has been restricted to a region of 2,050 bp spanning from intron 2 to intron 3.

checks.claim: The CISD2 exon 2 deletion included the codons for amino acids 102 to 106 within the 2Fe-2S domain.
checks.evidence_quote: Genomic data from our subjects show that the triplets coding for aminoacids WRSKT, from the position 102 to 106 of the polypeptide, are within the deleted region
checks.explanation: 2Fe-2S domain is stated as aa 99 to 112, so 102-106 fall within it.

checks.claim: Mozzillo et al. (2014) suggested that the CISD2 exon 2 deletion may produce a nonfunctional protein.
checks.evidence_quote: this may result in a non functional protein because of zinc-finger domain lost

checks.claim: The parents and brother of the WFS2 girl reported by Mozzillo et al. (2014) were heterozygous for the CISD2 exon 2 deletion.
checks.evidence_quote: The deletion was homozygous in the proband and heterozygous in her parents and brother.

checks.claim: The parents and brother heterozygous for the CISD2 exon 2 deletion had no ophthalmologic abnormalities, diabetes, or deafness.
checks.evidence_quote: Ophtalmological abnormalities, DM and deafness were not found in the parents and brother, whereas a reversible PA in response to ADP was found.

checks.claim: The parents and brother heterozygous for the CISD2 exon 2 deletion had a reversible platelet aggregation defect in response to ADP.
checks.evidence_quote: Ophtalmological abnormalities, DM and deafness were not found in the parents and brother, whereas a reversible PA in response to ADP was found.
